title: Prefix econometrics blueprint: hit-rate modeling, TTL synth, and safe rollout orchestration
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Problem: We are incurring unnecessary token/GPU costs from cache-miss heavy request tail and suboptimal per-prefix TTLs. Current TTL policies are coarse-grained and applied manually which leads to either over-caching (stale entries, wasted memory) or under-caching (higher inference load). Goal: produce an automated recommendation engine and safe apply flow that generates per-prefix TTLs and cache-key shaping suggestions using a hit-rate econometric model, verifies them in shadow/simulated environments, and then orchestrates staged rollout with automatic rollback gates.

Scope: hit-rate modeling for prefix-level keys (including affix/cohort bucketing), TTL synthesis (cohort + enforcement caps), cache-key design heuristics (affix normalization, collision mitigation), a simulation harness to forecast cost/latency tradeoffs for candidate policies, and a safe apply orchestration that integrates with rollout tooling (shadow canary, traffic ramp, automatic rollback). This ticket covers the modeling, policy generation, rollout playbook, and basic console UI hooks for human review.

Approach: 
- Data collection: sample prefix-access traces from edge logs and serving runtime (kv.lookup, miss latency, token counts) with a 7–14 day sliding window. Enrich with request metadata (route, model, sequence length bucket).
- Modeling: build a hierarchical hit-rate model per-prefix that estimates p_hit(t) as a function of inter-arrival time, request cohort, and request-context decay. Initial implementation: time-windowed Poisson/Negative-Binomial arrival model with empirical Bayesian shrinkage to pool low-frequency prefixes into cohort estimates. Output: expected hit-rate curve and marginal benefit curve (delta cost per token saved as TTL increases).
- TTL synthesis: compute an optimized TTL per-prefix (or per-cohort) by maximizing expected cost savings while bounding expected additional memory and stale-response risk. Enforce global caps (minTTL=1s, maxTTL=86_400s) and per-shard memory budget constraints. Provide a conservative and an aggressive candidate policy for each prefix.
- Cache key design: identify high-collision patterns and recommend canonicalization transforms (strip timestamps, normalize user-agent tokens, truncate long IDs) and namespace separation for privacy-sensitive keys. Generate example transform rules and test harness for verifying collision impact.
- Simulation & safety: run policy candidates through a simulator that replays sampled traffic with KV semantics (TTL, eviction, capacity) to estimate token cost, miss-ratio, latency impact, and memory footprint. Simulator must support stochastic arrival replay and return confidence intervals.
- Rollout orchestration: integrate with the existing rollout controller to implement a staged apply: shadow run -> 1% traffic canary (observability + cost delta) -> progressive ramp (1%->5%->20%->100%) with automatic rollback triggers (miss-rate spike, latency increase >X p50/p99, cost delta out of expected bound, or customer_impact flagged). Provide a manual abort path.
- Observability: surface per-prefix baseline vs candidate hit-rate, estimated savings, expected memory delta, and a synthetic backtest plot in Console Optimize. Expose alerts and a short-lived trial dashboard during canary.

Deliverables:
- Hit-rate estimator service + training job (Python/Go endpoints) and serialized cohort maps.
- TTL recommendation engine that emits policy artifacts (JSON TTL manifests) and scoring metadata.
- Simulation harness (replay + confidence intervals).
- Rollout playbook and orchestration hooks (shadow config, canary schedule, rollback thresholds).
- Console Optimize wiring: review screen with diffs and expected savings.
- Documentation: README + ops runbook for safe rollback and post-mortem checklist.

Why this is different: rather than a one-off ttl tuning tool, this work treats TTL as an econometric decision problem with uncertainty and explicit safety gates. The model prioritizes expected marginal savings per memory unit and produces conservative/aggressive policy pairs to match risk appetite.
acceptance_criteria: Simulator runs on 10M-sample traffic slice and reports expected token-cost delta with 95% CI
Recommendation engine emits per-prefix + per-cohort TTL manifests and a paired conservative/aggressive candidate
Console page renders review diff with expected cost savings and memory impact for the selected policy
Shadow run completes on staging with no performance regressions and the canary automation can perform staged ramps and auto-rollback based on thresholds
End-to-end test: rollout of a conservative policy on a small internal tenant shows measured cost savings within simulated CI and no p99 latency regression
risks: Model overfits short-term burst patterns and suggests overly aggressive TTLs leading to cache misses when burst fades
Cache key canonicalization may introduce collisions if transform rules are too aggressive
Simulator mismatch: replayed traffic may not capture cross-tenant interference or rare long-tail sequences
Rollback automation incorrectly thresholds and either rolls back unnecessarily or fails to roll back when needed
Memory pressure on KV shards if global caps are not enforced during rollout
notes: 2026-03-10: Kickoff meeting. Agreed on 14-day data window and cohort bucketing schema. Diego to own prototype hit-model.
2026-03-11: Data sampling job created by Data Eng. Initial prefix cardinality: ~1.2M unique keys in 7 days; top 0.5% account for 60% of misses.
2026-03-12: Prototype hit-model (NB) trained on 1M prefixes; shows good calibration on frequent prefixes but high variance on tail — adding hierarchical prior.
2026-03-14: Simulator skeleton implemented. Next: run 10M-sample replay and compute candidate TTL manifests. Plan to demo to Product & SRE on 2026-03-18.
